dengue.overview: Dengue is a mosquito-borne flavivirus infection endemic across tropical and subtropical regions. An estimated 100–400 million infections occur annually (WHO). Early diagnosis guides fluid management and case classification.
dengue.methods: NS1 antigen (early, day 1–7) · IgM/IgG serology (later, ~day 3–5+) · combined NS1+IgM/IgG for the widest window. RT-PCR for confirmation.
dengue.interpretation: NS1 positive = acute infection; IgM/IgG positive = recent or past exposure. Flavivirus cross-reactivity (Zika) must be considered in serology.
dengue.window: NS1: day 1–7 of fever (early). IgM: ~day 3–5. IgG: later, persists.
dengue.confirmatory: RT-PCR (viral RNA) is the reference; paired serology on acute and convalescent samples.
dengue.false_considerations: False negative: testing outside the marker window (IgM too early, NS1 too late). False positive: flavivirus cross-reactivity (Zika, yellow fever).
dengue.clinical_context: Caused by dengue virus (DENV 1–4), transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms: sudden high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia and rash. An estimated 100–400 million infections occur annually (WHO).
dengue.workflow: Clinically suspected dengue → NS1 antigen (early) or IgM/IgG (later) → confirm by PCR where available → classify severity to guide fluid management.
dengue.antigen_vs_antibody: NS1 antigen detects the virus itself (active infection, day 1–7); IgM/IgG detect the immune response (from ~day 3–5). A combined NS1+IgM/IgG device covers the full window.
dengue.settings: Rapid tests suit field clinics and outbreak response (instrument-free, minutes); reference labs confirm by PCR and serotype.
dengue.sources: WHO dengue guidelines; CDC dengue clinical guidance.

malaria.overview: Malaria is a parasitic infection by Plasmodium species transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. WHO recommends rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) where microscopy is unavailable.
malaria.methods: HRP2 (P. falciparum-specific) · pLDH (Pan-Plasmodium) · combined Pf/Pan or Pf/Pv devices for species differentiation.
malaria.interpretation: Pf-positive RDT + fever = treat for P. falciparum. HRP2 can persist after treatment; HRP2 gene deletions can cause false negatives.
malaria.window: RDTs detect antigen during active parasitemia, typically from symptom onset.
malaria.confirmatory: Microscopy (thin/thick smear) is the reference for species and parasitemia.
malaria.false_considerations: False negative: low parasitemia or HRP2 gene deletion. False positive: persistent HRP2 antigenemia after treatment.
malaria.clinical_context: Caused by Plasmodium parasites (P. falciparum most severe, P. vivax with liver-stage relapse), transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes. Symptoms: cyclic fever, chills, headache, anemia.
malaria.workflow: Fever in an endemic area → rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy → identify species → treat (ACT, plus anti-relapse for P. vivax).
malaria.antigen_vs_antibody: RDTs detect parasite antigens — HRP2 (P. falciparum) and pLDH (pan-Plasmodium). Serology is not used for acute diagnosis.
malaria.settings: RDTs enable field diagnosis where microscopy is unavailable; microscopy remains the reference for parasitemia and species confirmation.
malaria.sources: WHO malaria guidelines (2024); CDC malaria diagnosis.

hiv-std.overview: HIV and syphilis are bloodborne/sexually transmitted infections. Screening is standard in antenatal care, blood donation and key-population programs.
hiv-std.methods: Antibody tests (HIV-1/2, treponemal syphilis) · HIV p24 antigen · combined HIV/syphilis devices.
hiv-std.interpretation: A reactive HIV/syphilis antibody result is presumptive and must be confirmed per national algorithms (HIV: serial tests; syphilis: non-treponemal RPR titer).
hiv-std.window: HIV antibody: ~3–6 weeks (window period). Syphilis treponemal antibody: ~2–6 weeks.
hiv-std.confirmatory: HIV: serial/differentiation algorithm. Syphilis: non-treponemal RPR/VDRL titer for staging.
hiv-std.false_considerations: False negative: window period before seroconversion. False positive: rare — always confirm per national algorithm.
hiv-std.clinical_context: HIV (retrovirus) and syphilis (Treponema pallidum) are bloodborne/sexually transmitted. Screening is standard in antenatal care, blood donation and key-population programs.
hiv-std.workflow: Antibody/antigen screening → reactive results confirmed by serial tests (HIV) or non-treponemal RPR titer (syphilis) → linkage to care.
hiv-std.antigen_vs_antibody: HIV p24 antigen appears earlier than antibodies (narrows the window); treponemal syphilis antibodies persist after treatment.
hiv-std.settings: Rapid tests serve antenatal clinics, blood banks and outreach; laboratory confirmation follows national algorithms.
hiv-std.sources: WHO HIV testing services; CDC syphilis testing.

hepatitis.overview: Viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E) is a major global burden. HBsAg and anti-HCV are the core screening markers; HAV/HEV IgM indicate acute infection.
hepatitis.methods: HBsAg (surface antigen) · anti-HCV (antibody) · HAV IgM · HEV IgG/IgM · combo cassettes.
hepatitis.interpretation: HBsAg positive = HBV infection (acute or chronic). Anti-HCV positive = exposure, NOT active infection — confirm with HCV RNA.
hepatitis.window: HBsAg: earliest HBV marker. Anti-HCV: ~4–10 weeks after exposure.
hepatitis.confirmatory: Anti-HCV reactive → HCV RNA. HBsAg reactive → HBV DNA/panel.
hepatitis.false_considerations: False negative: anti-HCV window period. False positive: anti-HCV persists after viral clearance.
hepatitis.clinical_context: Viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E) is a major global burden. HBsAg and anti-HCV are the core screening markers; HAV/HEV IgM indicate acute infection.
hepatitis.workflow: Screen HBsAg + anti-HCV → confirm active infection (HBV DNA / HCV RNA) → stage liver disease and treat.
hepatitis.antigen_vs_antibody: HBsAg is a viral antigen (active infection); anti-HCV is an antibody (exposure, not active infection — needs RNA confirmation).
hepatitis.settings: Rapid tests suit screening programs and antenatal care; molecular confirmation is lab-based.
hepatitis.sources: WHO hepatitis testing guidelines; CDC viral hepatitis.

hpylori.overview: Helicobacter pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa and is linked to gastritis, peptic ulcer and gastric cancer. Non-invasive testing supports test-and-treat strategies.
hpylori.methods: Stool antigen (active infection) · serology (antibody, exposure) · urea breath test (reference non-invasive).
hpylori.interpretation: Stool antigen detects active infection and is suitable for post-treatment confirmation; serology cannot distinguish active from past infection.
hpylori.window: Stool antigen detectable during active colonization; PPI/antibiotic washout before testing.
hpylori.confirmatory: Urea breath test or endoscopy with biopsy.
hpylori.false_considerations: False negative: recent PPI or antibiotic use suppresses antigen. False positive: antibody serology stays positive after eradication.
hpylori.clinical_context: Helicobacter pylori colonizes gastric mucosa, linked to gastritis, peptic ulcer and gastric cancer. Non-invasive testing supports test-and-treat.
hpylori.workflow: Symptomatic patient → stool antigen (active) or urea breath test → treat → test-of-cure after eradication.
hpylori.antigen_vs_antibody: Stool antigen detects active infection (suitable for test-of-cure); antibody serology detects exposure and cannot distinguish active from past.
hpylori.settings: Stool antigen suits clinics running test-and-treat; urea breath test is the reference non-invasive test.
hpylori.sources: Maastricht VI/Florence consensus (2022); ACG H. pylori guideline.

respiratory.overview: COVID-19, influenza and RSV are the major seasonal respiratory viruses. Rapid antigen tests support syndromic diagnosis and triage.
respiratory.methods: Antigen tests (SARS-CoV-2, Influenza A/B, RSV) · multiplex combo devices · RT-PCR for confirmation.
respiratory.interpretation: Antigen tests are fast but less sensitive than molecular; a negative result during high prevalence does not exclude infection.
respiratory.window: Antigen best in the early symptomatic phase (first few days of symptoms).
respiratory.false_considerations: False negative: low viral load or late sampling. False positive: rare; confirm clinically or by PCR if discordant.
respiratory.clinical_context: COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2), influenza A/B and RSV are the major seasonal respiratory viruses with overlapping symptoms.
respiratory.workflow: Syndromic presentation → multiplex antigen test (COVID/Flu/RSV) → PCR confirmation where needed → isolation/treatment decisions.
respiratory.antigen_vs_antibody: Antigen tests detect viral proteins (active infection); antibody tests are not used for acute respiratory diagnosis.
respiratory.settings: Multiplex antigen tests suit clinics and emergency departments; PCR is the lab reference.
respiratory.sources: WHO COVID-19 guidance; CDC influenza & RSV.

cardiac.overview: Cardiac biomarkers support the diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction and other cardiac conditions. Troponin is the preferred marker.
cardiac.methods: Troponin I/T · CK-MB · Myoglobin · H-FABP · D-Dimer (thrombosis) · CRP/PCT/SAA (inflammation).
cardiac.interpretation: Point-of-care assays are triage-grade; serial testing and clinical correlation are required. D-Dimer is for VTE exclusion, not diagnosis.
cardiac.window: Troponin rises ~3–6 h after myocardial injury, peaks ~12–24 h.
cardiac.confirmatory: Serial high-sensitivity troponin + ECG + clinical assessment.
cardiac.false_considerations: False negative: testing before the ~3–6 h troponin rise. False positive: non-MI causes of troponin elevation (renal failure, myocarditis).
cardiac.clinical_context: Acute myocardial infarction and heart failure drive cardiac biomarker testing. Troponin is the preferred marker; BNP/NT-proBNP for heart failure.
cardiac.workflow: Chest pain → serial troponin + ECG → diagnose MI (rise/fall pattern) → risk-stratify and treat.
cardiac.antigen_vs_antibody: Cardiac tests detect proteins (troponin, CK-MB, myoglobin), not antibodies — a key difference from infectious-disease serology.
cardiac.settings: POC troponin triages in emergency settings; high-sensitivity lab assays are the diagnostic standard.
cardiac.sources: ESC/ACC universal definition of MI; NICE chest pain guidance.

doa-workplace.overview: Drug-of-abuse testing supports workplace screening, clinical toxicology and rehabilitation programs. Urine is the standard specimen.
doa-workplace.methods: Single-analyte tests (THC, COC, AMP, MET, MOP/OPI, BZO, Fentanyl, etc.) · multi-panel cups (2–14 analytes) with adulteration checks.
doa-workplace.interpretation: Screening results are presumptive; any positive analyte requires confirmatory testing (GC-MS/LC-MS). Cut-offs align with regulatory (SAMHSA-style) standards.
doa-workplace.window: Detection window varies by analyte (hours to days); urine is the standard specimen.
doa-workplace.confirmatory: GC-MS / LC-MS for any presumptive positive.
doa-workplace.false_considerations: False negative: diluted or adulterated urine. False positive: cross-reactivity with related compounds.
doa-workplace.clinical_context: Drug-of-abuse testing supports workplace screening, clinical toxicology and rehabilitation. Urine is the standard specimen.
doa-workplace.workflow: Screening (immunoassay) → any presumptive positive → confirmatory GC-MS/LC-MS → report per cut-offs.
doa-workplace.antigen_vs_antibody: DOA tests are competitive immunoassays detecting drug/metabolite, not antibody-based.
doa-workplace.settings: Workplace, occupational health and clinical toxicology; confirmation is laboratory-based.

pregnancy-fertility.overview: Reproductive hormone tests support pregnancy detection and fertility tracking.
pregnancy-fertility.methods: hCG (pregnancy) · LH (ovulation) · FSH (menopause/fertility) · fFN and iGFBP-1 (preterm risk) · PDG.
pregnancy-fertility.interpretation: hCG positive = pregnancy; LH surge predicts ovulation ~24–36h later. fFN/iGFBP-1 are risk-stratification aids, not diagnostic.
pregnancy-fertility.window: hCG: from ~day of missed period. LH surge: mid-cycle, precedes ovulation ~24–36 h.
pregnancy-fertility.false_considerations: False negative: testing before the hCG rise / LH surge. False positive: rare.
pregnancy-fertility.clinical_context: Reproductive hormone tests support pregnancy detection and fertility tracking across retail and clinical channels.
pregnancy-fertility.workflow: hCG for pregnancy; LH surge for ovulation timing; FSH for ovarian reserve/menopause; fFN/iGFBP-1 for preterm-risk stratification.
pregnancy-fertility.antigen_vs_antibody: These are hormone (antigen) tests, not antibody tests.
pregnancy-fertility.settings: Retail (hCG/LH) and clinical (FSH, fFN, iGFBP-1) use; confirmation by ultrasound or quantitative hCG.

tumor.overview: Tumor markers are proteins associated with certain cancers, used in screening support and monitoring of high-risk groups.
tumor.interpretation: Elevated tumor markers are not diagnostic of cancer — imaging and confirmatory testing are required; markers also rise in benign conditions.
tumor.window: Not time-critical; used in screening support and serial monitoring.
tumor.confirmatory: Imaging and biopsy; markers are not diagnostic alone.
tumor.false_considerations: False negative: non-secreting tumors. False positive: markers also rise in benign conditions.
tumor.clinical_context: Tumor markers are proteins associated with certain cancers, used in screening support and monitoring, not standalone diagnosis.
tumor.workflow: Elevated marker (PSA/AFP/CEA) → imaging + biopsy → confirmed diagnosis → serial monitoring.
tumor.antigen_vs_antibody: Tumor-marker tests detect proteins (antigens); some autoimmune serology (RF) uses antibody detection.
tumor.settings: Screening support and monitoring in clinics and labs; imaging/biopsy are definitive.

tropical.overview: Tropical and neglected diseases include chikungunya, Zika, leptospirosis, leishmaniasis, Chagas, filariasis, typhoid, cholera and tuberculosis.
tropical.methods: IgM/IgG serology · antigen tests (cholera O1/O139, typhoid Ag) · combined panels.
tropical.interpretation: Serology cross-reactivity is common among tropical pathogens; results require epidemiological context and confirmation where available.
tropical.window: Varies by pathogen; serology typically detects antibodies 1–2+ weeks after onset.
tropical.confirmatory: PCR, culture, or paired serology depending on the pathogen.
tropical.false_considerations: False negative: serology sampled before antibodies appear. False positive: cross-reactivity among tropical pathogens.
tropical.clinical_context: Tropical and neglected diseases — chikungunya, Zika, leptospirosis, leishmaniasis, Chagas, filariasis, typhoid, cholera, TB — overlap in fever syndromes.
tropical.workflow: Fever with travel/exposure history → serology or antigen testing → confirm by PCR/culture where available → epidemiological context required.
tropical.antigen_vs_antibody: Serology (IgM/IgG) is common but cross-reactive; antigen tests (cholera O1/O139, typhoid) detect active pathogen.
tropical.settings: Field and reference-laboratory testing; confirmation depends on the pathogen.
tropical.sources: WHO neglected tropical disease and outbreak guidance.

gastrointestinal.overview: Gastrointestinal infections (viral, bacterial, parasitic) and inflammatory bowel markers are common point-of-care needs.
gastrointestinal.methods: Rotavirus/Adenovirus/Norovirus antigen · C. difficile (GDH + toxin) · Giardia/Cryptosporidium · Calprotectin/Lactoferrin (IBD) · FOB.
gastrointestinal.interpretation: Antigen detection indicates active shedding; calprotectin/lactoferrin support IBD vs functional distinction, not diagnosis alone.
gastrointestinal.window: Antigen detectable during active pathogen shedding.
gastrointestinal.confirmatory: Culture or molecular (PCR) testing where required.
gastrointestinal.false_considerations: False negative: intermittent pathogen shedding. False positive: rare.
gastrointestinal.clinical_context: Gastrointestinal infections (viral, bacterial, parasitic) and inflammatory markers are common point-of-care needs.
gastrointestinal.workflow: Diarrhea → antigen testing (rotavirus/adenovirus/norovirus, C. difficile GDH+toxin, parasites) → culture/molecular confirmation where needed.
gastrointestinal.antigen_vs_antibody: Antigen tests detect active shedding; calprotectin/lactoferrin measure gut inflammation (IBD vs IBS).
gastrointestinal.settings: Clinics and labs; C. difficile uses a two-step GDH+toxin algorithm.
gastrointestinal.sources: IDSA C. difficile guideline; WHO diarrheal-disease guidance.
